key_features.classic_presentation: Acute hepatitis presents with RUQ discomfort, fatigue, nausea, jaundice (yellow skin/eyes), dark urine, pale stools. Onset over days to weeks. Viral (A, B, C), drug-induced, or autoimmune. Tender hepatomegaly on exam.
key_features.typical_demographics: Viral: young adults. Drug-induced: any age, medication exposure. Alcoholic: chronic heavy drinking.
key_features.pathophysiology_brief: Hepatocellular injury and inflammation from viral infection, drugs (acetaminophen, medications), alcohol, or autoimmune.

diagnostic_questions.context: Jaundice is hallmark when bilirubin >3. May notice eyes first.
Dark urine (bili rubinuria) often precedes jaundice.
RUQ discomfort/fullness, not severe pain. Severe pain suggests other diagnosis.
Fatigue and malaise often prominent, sometimes preceding jaundice.
Ask about: medications, alcohol, drug use, exposures, travel.
Onset over days to weeks, not acute hours.

differential_diagnosis.key_difference: Severe RUQ pain, fever, acute onset
Severe pain, rapid jaundice, Charcot's triad

red_flags.action: Acute liver failure - ICU level care required
Possible fulminant hepatic failure - urgent care, consider N-acetylcysteine

typical_management: Supportive care. Stop offending agents (alcohol, medications). Viral: rest, hydration. Drug-induced: stop drug, NAC if acetaminophen. Monitor liver enzymes, coags.
disposition: Mild: outpatient with close follow-up. Moderate-severe: admission. Acute liver failure: ICU.
patient_education: Hepatitis is liver inflammation. Causes include viruses, medications, and alcohol. Most viral hepatitis resolves with supportive care. Avoid alcohol and unnecessary medications during recovery.
